In the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple has taken the next step toward its long-standing vision of turning the iPhone into a single sheet of glass: embedding the Face ID module beneath the display.

Achieving this without letting the Face ID components show through the screen, while also not compromising display quality in that area, requires quite ingenious engineering……

Jony Ive once described the iPhone design vision as a single slab of glass in the early years. Although he has since left the company, that goal has continued. Apple ultimately hopes to hide all the technology that needs to occupy screen space—including Face ID and the front-facing camera—entirely beneath the display.

The iPhone 18 Pro has become the first to deliver on the former, but the process has been far from easy. Face ID requires the TrueDepth module to both project and receive infrared light, and infrared cannot pass through display pixels.

Apple had to create gaps between the pixels large enough for the infrared to pass through, while at the same time not allowing screen quality to visibly degrade. To achieve this, the company's engineers set about designing an entirely new pixel layout that increases the spacing between pixels without affecting the display output.

iFixit demonstrated this pixel arrangement under a microscope, and Apple also confirmed to me that the overall pixel density within the module's area has been cut in half. This could have created a second problem: halving the pixel density would likely make that region of the screen noticeably dimmer, so Apple compensated by boosting the brightness of those pixels. At the same time, the assembly appears to include an infrared filter to block visible light from passing through the gaps, further concealing the components beneath.

The result is astonishing. In actual use, even if you stare at it extremely closely, you can barely detect the presence of the TrueDepth camera assembly. I've tried macro photography under different screen colour and lighting conditions, and I couldn't capture it. This doesn't mean it's completely undetectable—iFixit's microscope images have proven otherwise—but in everyday use, you will absolutely not notice its presence.

This achievement has reduced the size of the Dynamic Island, which in turn allows the iPhone to display three Live Activities simultaneously, one more than before. In some future iPhone model, the front-facing camera will also be hidden beneath the display. Technically this is already achievable, but the sacrifice in image quality currently remains beyond what Apple is willing to accept. Solving this is a matter of when, not whether.
